title: Prices, the market, and bargaining
goal: Ask the price, bargain without sounding rude, and complete a whole purchase at the market — all in krama, because that is the right level for an older stallholder.
bekal: ask the price with *pira regané* / *pinten reginipun*
bargain with *kirang* and *mangga* without sounding pushy

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Ing peken Kranggan
dialogs.intro: Dian goes shopping with Rini at Kranggan Market. The stallholder, Mbak Sri, is much older — so Dian uses krama. Notice that Mbak Sri answers in a mix of ngoko and krama, and that's normal: an older seller doesn't have to step up to krama.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Nuwun sèwu, Mbak. Gedhang menika pinten reginipun?
lines.id: Excuse me, Mbak. How much are these bananas?
lines.literal: beg thousand, Mbak. banana this how-much price-its?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.id: Couldn't you make it a bit less?

lines.speaker: Mbak Sri:
lines.text: Sepuluh èwu waé, wis. Sing iki isih anyar kok.
lines.id: Ten thousand, then, fine. These are still fresh, you know.
lines.literal: ten thousand just, done. which this still new kok.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Inggih, kula pendhet kalih sisir. Lombokipun pinten sekilo?
lines.id: All right, I'll take two bunches. How much are the chilies per kilo?
lines.literal: yes, I take two bunch. chili-the how-much one-kilo?

lines.speaker: Mbak Sri:
lines.text: Lombok abang selawé èwu, lombok ijo wolulas.
lines.id: Red chilies are twenty-five thousand, green ones eighteen.
lines.literal: chili red twenty-five thousand, chili green eighteen.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.id: That's expensive. Just half a kilo, then.

lines.speaker: Mbak Sri:
lines.text: Iya. Sedaya dados telung puluh telung èwu.
lines.id: Sure. That makes thirty-three thousand altogether.
lines.literal: yes. all become thirty three thousand.

lines.speaker: Mbak Sri:
lines.text: Susukipun pitulas èwu. Matur nuwun, nggih.
lines.id: Your change is seventeen thousand. Thank you.
lines.literal: change-the seventeen thousand. thank you, yes.

notes: **Mangga** is one of the most useful words in all of Javanese, and its meaning shifts with the situation: "please, go ahead", "come on", "excuse me", "let's", and — said as you walk off — "I'll be going". The ngoko forms are *ayo* or *monggo* (a casual spelling of *mangga*). If you learn only ten Javanese words, make this one of them.

**Nggih** is the casual form of *inggih* (yes), and it's very often tacked onto the end of a sentence as a softener, much like "…, right?" or "…, OK?" in English: *awis nggih* (that's pricey, isn't it), *matur nuwun nggih*. The ngoko form is *ya*.

**Mawon** is the krama for *waé* (just, only); its full form is often written *kémawon*. It's used constantly to soften a request: *setengah kilo mawon* ("just half a kilo") sounds much gentler than a bare *setengah kilo*.

**Kok** at the end of a sentence is not a question word. It's an emphatic "you know, actually", used to gently contradict what the other person seems to think: *isih anyar kok* — "they're still fresh, you know".
**Dados** (krama) and **dadi** (ngoko) mean "become". In this dialogue it means "the total comes to". It also works as the linking word "so": *dadi aku ora lunga* (so I didn't go).
**Pendhet** (krama) / **jupuk** (ngoko) means "take". At the market, saying *kula pendhet kalih* ("I'll take two") is the standard way to close the bargaining and show that you're buying.
**Susuk** means "change" (the money you get back) — one handy word. The krama is also *susuk*; only the ending changes, to *susukipun*.

grammars.title: Asking and giving prices
body: Several patterns are all correct and used interchangeably. Pick one, memorize it, and you can already go shopping.
after: **Tak** in front of a verb means "I" as the one doing the action — *tak jupuk* (I'll take), *tak tuku* (I'll buy), *tak deleng* (I'll look). It's a very typically Javanese form and is covered fully in Unit 18. For now, learn these as fixed chunks.

**Éntuk** means "may, be allowed" (krama *angsal*), unlike *bisa*, which means "be able" (krama *saged*). *Ora éntuk* = not allowed; *ora bisa* = not able. Like English "can", everyday speech often blurs the two, so take care here.

blocks.text: Market units are simple: put the prefix *sa-* / *se-*, meaning "one", in front of the unit:

head: Unit
Used for
Example
rows: *kangkung seiket* — a bundle of water spinach
*sega sabungkus* — a wrapped portion of rice
*ès tèh sagelas* — a glass of iced tea

blocks.text: Bargaining at a Javanese market isn't a fight; it's a conversation. Sellers expect it, and bargaining gently often gets you a better price than pushing. These three sentences cover everything you need.

items: **Menapa boten saged kirang, Bu?** — "Couldn't you make it less, ma'am?" The standard opener. Say it with a smile, not a demanding tone.
**Kirangi sekedhik nggih.** — "Take a little off, OK?" Even softer, because it names no number and leaves the decision to the seller.
**Kalih dasa mawon pripun?** — "How about just twenty?" It names a number, but wrapping it in the question *pripun* (how about) keeps it from sounding like an ultimatum.

blocks.title: Unwritten rules
items: **Don't bargain over things that are obviously cheap**, like a bundle of vegetables for a thousand rupiah. Haggling over a thousand rupiah reads as an insult, not thrift.
**If you've bargained and the seller agrees, you must buy.** Bargaining and then walking away is the one thing market etiquette treats as truly rude.
**Close with *matur nuwun* and *mangga*.** Those two words turn a transaction into an acquaintance, and market sellers remember faces — tomorrow's price may differ because of it.
Nuwun sèwu, Bu. Lombok menika ____ reginipun? (how much)
